sections.name: A. Tools and basic floors
sections.purpose: Turn scores into information, then information and bits into risk.
sections.guide: Read the score identity, data processing, trace chain rule, van Trees bound, sample/bit floors, and leftover-entropy budget. Keep the definitions and constants in (85), (86), (96), and (116). The prior integrals (87)-(95) and van Trees proof (97)-(100) can wait once you retain their conclusions in (85) and (101).

sections.name: B. Rare events and score shifts
sections.purpose: A rare transcript event shifts a score mean; bits bound the surprisal cost.
sections.guide: Understand the event-score bounds (121)-(123), their tail assumptions (120), and the surprisal second moment (139). Read (128) and (130) for the proof idea. Tilt arithmetic (132)-(135) and tail integration (140)-(144) can wait; retain the endpoint bounds, including their conditioning requirements.

sections.name: C. Independent private blocks
sections.purpose: The rectangle structure keeps blocks conditionally independent and cancels cross terms.
sections.guide: This is the structural heart of the converse. Follow the rectangle (150), product posterior (153), and information sum (159). Important links are (152), (157), (158), (162), and (165): surprisal adds, cross terms cancel, and the bit budget controls the remaining correction. Seed averaging (166)-(167) can wait.

sections.name: D. Overlap and shared data
sections.purpose: Reveal shared samples in the proof, then apply the independent-block result to private data.
sections.guide: Learn the shared/private partition (170) and the information bounds (174), (176), and (192). Read (172), (181), (182), (184), and (188) to see why the reduction is valid. Averaging steps (185)-(187) can wait. Check the zero-private-data case (191) when that edge case matters.

sections.name: E. Close the converse
sections.purpose: Combine Fisher and entropy ceilings, cancel localization, and solve for the risk floor.
sections.guide: Trace (197)+(198) through localization cancellation (202), the scalar log inequality (206), and the refinement floor (219), then combine all floors in (220). Keep the variable changes (200), (205), and the inversion idea (211). Constant calculations (199), (207)-(208), (226), and case algebra (214)-(218) can wait. For the sharper Gaussian branch (221)-(230), focus on (227), the Lambert inverse (229), and the final bound (230).
